title: Photosynthesis in Higher Plants
description: Grade 11 Biology: site and pigments of photosynthesis, the light reaction and photophosphorylation, the Calvin cycle (dark reaction), C3 vs C4 plants and factors affecting photosynthesis.

topics.title: Site, Pigments and the Light Reaction
topics.concept:
Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants make their own food (glucose) from carbon dioxide and water, using light energy, and release oxygen. It is the source of nearly all the food and oxygen on Earth. The overall equation is:

6CO₂ + 12H₂O →(light, chlorophyll) C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ + 6H₂O

Photosynthesis takes place in the chloroplasts, mostly in the leaf mesophyll. A chloroplast has stacks of flattened sacs called grana (made of thylakoids) sitting in a fluid called the stroma. The light-trapping pigments are in the thylakoid membranes; the main pigment is chlorophyll a, helped by accessory pigments (chlorophyll b, carotenoids) that absorb light and pass the energy to chlorophyll a.

Photosynthesis has two stages. The first is the light reaction (photochemical phase), which happens in the thylakoid membranes and needs light. Here:

  • Light energy is absorbed and used to split water — photolysis — releasing oxygen (the O₂ we breathe comes from water, not CO₂).
  • The energy is stored in the molecules ATP and NADPH. Making ATP using light is called photophosphorylation.

So the light reaction produces the "assimilatory power" (ATP + NADPH) and oxygen.

examples.problem: Example 1: In which organelle and which part does the light reaction occur?
examples.solution:
Locate the light reaction.

  • It occurs in the chloroplast.
  • Specifically in the thylakoid membranes (grana).
examples.answer: In the chloroplast, in the thylakoid membranes (grana).

examples.problem: Example 2: From which molecule does the oxygen released in photosynthesis come?
examples.solution:
Recall photolysis.

  • Water is split (photolysis) in the light reaction.
  • The oxygen comes from water, not carbon dioxide.
examples.answer: The oxygen comes from the splitting of water (photolysis), not from CO₂.

examples.problem: Example 3: Name the two energy-rich products of the light reaction.
examples.solution:
The light reaction stores energy.

  • ATP and NADPH (the assimilatory power).

recap:
• Photosynthesis: CO₂ + H₂O + light → glucose + O₂; happens in chloroplasts (grana/thylakoids in stroma).
  • Main pigment chlorophyll a; accessory pigments pass energy to it.
  • Light reaction (thylakoid membrane): splits water (photolysis → O₂), makes ATP + NADPH.
  • Oxygen released comes from water.

quiz.q: The oxygen released during photosynthesis comes from:
quiz.explanation: Photolysis of water releases the oxygen.

quiz.q: The light reaction takes place in the:
quiz.explanation: The light reaction occurs in the thylakoid membranes of the grana.

topics.title: The Dark Reaction (Calvin Cycle) and C3 vs C4 Plants
topics.concept:
The second stage is the dark reaction (biosynthetic phase), also called the Calvin cycle. Despite the name, it does not require darkness — it simply does not directly use light. It takes place in the stroma of the chloroplast and uses the ATP and NADPH made in the light reaction to fix carbon dioxide into sugar.

In the Calvin cycle, CO₂ is added to a 5-carbon acceptor molecule (RuBP) by the enzyme RuBisCO — the most abundant enzyme on Earth. Through a series of steps using ATP and NADPH, this builds up glucose, and the acceptor RuBP is regenerated to keep the cycle going. Because the first stable product here is a 3-carbon compound (3-PGA), plants that fix carbon only this way are called C3 plants (e.g. wheat, rice).

Some plants in hot, dry climates use a clever extra step. They first fix CO₂ into a 4-carbon acid in their mesophyll cells, then release the CO₂ to the Calvin cycle inside special bundle-sheath cells. These are C4 plants (e.g. maize, sugarcane). C4 plants are more efficient in strong sunlight and high temperature, lose less water, and largely avoid the wasteful side reaction of RuBisCO called photorespiration. This special leaf structure in C4 plants is called Kranz anatomy.

examples.problem: Example 1: Where does the Calvin cycle take place, and what does it use from the light reaction?
examples.solution:
The dark reaction follows the light reaction.

  • It takes place in the stroma of the chloroplast.
  • It uses ATP and NADPH made in the light reaction.
examples.answer: In the stroma, using the ATP and NADPH produced by the light reaction.

examples.problem: Example 2: Why are wheat and rice called C3 plants?
examples.solution:
Look at the first stable product.

  • The first stable product of CO₂ fixation is a 3-carbon compound (3-PGA).
  • Hence they are called C3 plants.
examples.answer: Because the first stable product of CO₂ fixation is a 3-carbon compound (3-PGA).

examples.problem: Example 3: Give two advantages of C4 plants over C3 plants in hot, dry climates.
examples.solution:
C4 plants have an extra CO₂-concentrating step.

  • They photosynthesise efficiently in strong light/high temperature and lose less water.
  • They largely avoid photorespiration.
examples.answer: C4 plants are more efficient in strong light/heat, lose less water, and avoid photorespiration.

recap:
• Dark reaction = Calvin cycle, in the stroma; uses ATP + NADPH to fix CO₂ into sugar.
  • Enzyme RuBisCO fixes CO₂ onto RuBP; first stable product = 3-carbon (3-PGA).
  • C3 plants (wheat, rice) vs C4 plants (maize, sugarcane): C4 first makes a 4-carbon acid, use Kranz anatomy.
  • C4 = efficient in heat/light, less water loss, avoids photorespiration.

quiz.q: The Calvin cycle (dark reaction) takes place in the:
quiz.explanation: The dark reaction occurs in the stroma of the chloroplast.

quiz.q: The enzyme that fixes CO₂ in the Calvin cycle is:
quiz.explanation: RuBisCO fixes CO₂ onto RuBP — the most abundant enzyme on Earth.

topics.title: Factors Affecting Photosynthesis
topics.concept:
The rate of photosynthesis depends on conditions inside and outside the plant. The external factors are light, carbon dioxide, temperature and water; the internal factors include the amount of chlorophyll and the number and state of the leaves.

  • Light — the rate rises as light increases, up to a point, then levels off (at very high light it can even fall slightly).
  • Carbon dioxide — usually the most important limiting factor in nature; raising CO₂ increases the rate up to a saturation point. (This is why greenhouses sometimes add extra CO₂.)
  • Temperature — the reactions are enzyme-controlled, so the rate rises with temperature to an optimum and then falls as enzymes are denatured.
  • Water — a shortage closes stomata (reducing CO₂ intake) and slows growth, indirectly lowering the rate.

A key idea here is Blackman's Law of Limiting Factors: when a process depends on several factors, its rate is set by the factor that is in shortest supply — the limiting factor. For example, on a bright warm day with plenty of light and warmth, the rate may still be low simply because CO₂ is limited; adding more light will not help until the CO₂ supply is increased. Understanding limiting factors helps farmers and greenhouse growers boost crop yields by improving whatever is most lacking.

examples.problem: Example 1: Name any three external factors that affect the rate of photosynthesis.
examples.solution:
List the environmental factors.

  • Light, carbon dioxide and temperature (also water).
examples.answer: Light, carbon dioxide and temperature (water is also a factor).

examples.problem: Example 2: State Blackman's Law of Limiting Factors.
examples.solution:
The slowest factor controls the rate.

  • When a process depends on several factors, the rate is set by the factor in shortest supply (the limiting factor).
examples.answer: When several factors affect a process, its rate is determined by the one in shortest supply (the limiting factor).

examples.problem: Example 3: Why does the rate of photosynthesis fall at very high temperatures?
examples.solution:
The reactions use enzymes.

  • Photosynthesis is enzyme-controlled.
  • At very high temperatures the enzymes are denatured, so the rate falls.
examples.answer: Because the enzymes controlling photosynthesis get denatured at very high temperatures.

recap:
• External factors: light, CO₂, temperature, water; internal: chlorophyll, leaf state.
  • Rate rises then saturates with light and CO₂; rises to an optimum then falls with temperature (enzymes denature).
  • CO₂ is often the main limiting factor in nature.
  • Blackman's Law: the rate is set by the factor in shortest supply (limiting factor).

quiz.q: According to the law of limiting factors, the rate of photosynthesis is set by the factor that is:
quiz.explanation: The factor in shortest supply (the limiting factor) determines the rate.

quiz.q: The rate of photosynthesis falls at very high temperatures because:
quiz.explanation: Photosynthesis is enzyme-controlled; high heat denatures the enzymes.

questions.q: Photosynthesis takes place mainly in the:
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts are the site of photosynthesis.

questions.q: The main photosynthetic pigment is:
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll a is the main pigment; others are accessory pigments.

questions.q: The light reaction occurs in the:
questions.explanation: The light reaction happens in the thylakoid membranes.

questions.q: Splitting of water in the light reaction is called:
questions.explanation: Photolysis splits water, releasing oxygen.

questions.q: The oxygen released in photosynthesis comes from:
questions.explanation: Oxygen comes from the photolysis of water.

questions.q: The two energy-rich products of the light reaction are:
questions.explanation: The light reaction makes ATP and NADPH (assimilatory power).

questions.q: The dark reaction (Calvin cycle) occurs in the:
questions.explanation: The Calvin cycle takes place in the stroma.

questions.q: The CO₂-fixing enzyme of the Calvin cycle is:
questions.explanation: RuBisCO fixes CO₂ onto RuBP.

questions.q: In C3 plants, the first stable product of CO₂ fixation has:
questions.explanation: C3 plants form a 3-carbon compound (3-PGA) first.

questions.q: Which of these is a C4 plant?
questions.explanation: Maize (and sugarcane) are C4 plants.

questions.q: The special leaf anatomy of C4 plants is called:
questions.explanation: C4 plants show Kranz anatomy with bundle-sheath cells.

questions.q: The wasteful side reaction of RuBisCO largely avoided by C4 plants is:
questions.explanation: C4 plants concentrate CO₂ and avoid photorespiration.

questions.q: In nature, the factor that most often limits photosynthesis is:
questions.explanation: CO₂ is usually the main limiting factor in natural conditions.

questions.q: According to Blackman's law, the rate is determined by the factor that is:
questions.explanation: The limiting factor (in shortest supply) sets the rate.

questions.q: The rate of photosynthesis falls at very high temperatures because:
questions.explanation: High heat denatures the enzymes controlling photosynthesis.

questions.q: An experiment using heavy-oxygen-labelled water (H₂¹⁸O) shows the released O₂ is also labelled. This proves the oxygen comes from:
questions.explanation: The labelled oxygen appearing in O₂ proves it originates from water, not CO₂.

questions.q: If the light reaction is blocked, the Calvin cycle soon stops because it is deprived of:
questions.explanation: The dark reaction depends on the ATP and NADPH made by the light reaction.

questions.q: On a bright warm day with abundant light and warmth, photosynthesis may still be slow if CO₂ is low. This illustrates that:
options: The factor in shortest supply limits the rate
questions.explanation: With light and heat plentiful, low CO₂ becomes the limiting factor (Blackman's law).

questions.q: C4 plants such as sugarcane outperform C3 plants in hot climates mainly because they:
options: Concentrate CO₂ in bundle-sheath cells and avoid photorespiration
questions.explanation: The C4 pathway raises CO₂ around RuBisCO, suppressing photorespiration and boosting efficiency.

questions.q: Greenhouse growers sometimes pump extra CO₂ into the air because, up to a point, CO₂ is:
options: A limiting factor that increases the rate when raised
questions.explanation: Raising the limiting CO₂ increases photosynthesis up to saturation, improving yield.

questions.q: During a drought, photosynthesis slows even in bright light chiefly because water shortage causes:
options: Stomata to close, cutting CO₂ intake
The Calvin cycle to speed up
questions.explanation: Closed stomata limit CO₂ entry, indirectly lowering the rate during water stress.
